summary: The time prepositions take the genitive like every preposition: قَبْلَ (before), بَعْدَ (after), حَتَّى (until; from … to … = مِنْ … إِلَى …), مُنْذُ (since; for a period up to now), خِلَالَ and أَثْنَاءَ (during). قَبْلَ, بَعْدَ, خِلَالَ and أَثْنَاءَ are old nouns in the accusative, like أَمَامَ in lesson 12: they end in -a and take pronoun endings (قَبْلِي, بَعْدَكَ, خِلَالَهُ). “At / on / in” a time is فِي for all three — فِي السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ, فِي يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ, فِي يَنَايِرَ, فِي الصَّيْفِ — where German needs um / am / im; often no preposition is needed at all (يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ, صَيْفًا), and عِنْدَ marks a moment (عِنْدَ الظُّهْرِ). قَبْلَ + a span means “ago” (قَبْلَ سَنَةٍ), بَعْدَ + a span “in” (بَعْدَ أُسْبُوعٍ). مُنْذُ goes with the present for what is still going on — أَعِيشُ هُنَا مُنْذُ سَنَةٍ, exactly like German “ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier”. Arabic has no word for “o’clock”: the hour is السَّاعَةُ + a feminine ordinal, السَّاعَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ (“the fifth hour”). The months have two sets of names: old Syriac ones (كَانُونُ الثَّانِي, شُبَاطُ …) in Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine and Iraq, Latin ones (يَنَايِرُ, فِبْرَايِرُ …) in Egypt, Sudan and the Arabian Peninsula; a month name is a diptote: فِي يَنَايِرَ, فِي شُبَاطَ.

head: preposition
meaning
example
rows: أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ قَبْلَ الْفَطُورِ. — وَصَلْتُ قَبْلَ سَاعَةٍ.
نَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ بَعْدَ الْغَدَاءِ. — أُسَافِرُ بَعْدَ أُسْبُوعٍ.
أَنْتَظِرُ مُنْذُ الصَّبَاحِ. — أَعِيشُ هُنَا مُنْذُ سَنَةٍ.
فِي السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ — فِي يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ — فِي الصَّيْفِ
blocks.caption: All of them with the genitive.

head: meaning
Arabic
blocks.caption: One فِي — or the bare accusative — for at / on / in.

notes.text: English needs three prepositions — at five, on Monday, in May; Arabic has one فِي for all of them, or none.
German um / am / im all become فِي — or nothing: um fünf = فِي السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ, am Montag = يَوْمَ الِاثْنَيْنِ.
Greek uses στις for the hour (στις πέντε) and a bare accusative for days, months and seasons (τη Δευτέρα, τον Μάιο, το καλοκαίρι) — like the Arabic bare accusative يَوْمَ الِاثْنَيْنِ, صَيْفًا.
French à cinq heures, lundi, en mai, en été; Arabic: فِي for all, or the bare accusative.

head: time
Arabic
literally
blocks.caption: كَمِ السَّاعَةُ؟ — What time is it? There is no word for “o’clock”; in everyday speech the cardinal is common (السَّاعَة خَمْسَة).

head: Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine, Iraq
Egypt, Sudan, Arabian Peninsula
blocks.caption: The Syriac names go back to Babylonian months and are cousins of the Hebrew month names (שְׁבָט, אֲדָר, נִיסָן …); the others come from Latin. The Maghreb uses other forms again (جانفي, يوليوز …).

notes.text: The Latin-based set (يَنَايِر, فِبْرَايِر, مَارِس …) matches Ιανουάριος, Φεβρουάριος, Μάρτιος …
Algeria and Tunisia use month names taken from French: جانفي (janvier), جويلية (juillet), أوت (août).
Turkish Şubat, Nisan, Haziran, Temmuz, Eylül are the Syriac names شُبَاط, نَيْسَان, حَزِيرَان, تَمُّوز, أَيْلُول.
Iran uses its own solar months (فروردین, اردیبهشت …), related to neither Arabic set.

blocks.title: مُنْذُ + present.
blocks.text: For something that started in the past and still goes on, Arabic uses the present, like German seit: أَدْرُسُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ مُنْذُ سَنَةٍ = Ich lerne seit einem Jahr Arabisch. With a past verb مُنْذُ means “ago”: وَصَلَ مُنْذُ سَاعَةٍ.

notes.text: English uses the perfect (I have been learning Arabic for a year); Arabic uses the present: أَدْرُسُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ مُنْذُ سَنَةٍ.
French depuis + present is مُنْذُ + present: j’apprends l’arabe depuis un an.
Spanish desde hace + present (estudio árabe desde hace un año) is مُنْذُ + present.
Russian also uses the present here (я учу арабский уже год), like مُنْذُ + present.
Greek also uses the present (μαθαίνω αραβικά εδώ και ένα χρόνο), like مُنْذُ + present.

blocks.title: Before ≠ in front of.
blocks.text: قَبْلَ is time (قَبْلَ الْعَشَاءِ, before dinner); in front of a place is أَمَامَ (أَمَامَ الْبَيْتِ). After is بَعْدَ; behind is خَلْفَ / وَرَاءَ.

blocks.title: Ago and in.
blocks.text: قَبْلَ سَاعَةٍ = an hour ago; بَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ = in an hour; خِلَالَ سَاعَةٍ = within an hour.

items.title: خِلَالَ
points: the whole span: خِلَالَ الْأُسْبُوعِ (during the week)

items.title: أَثْنَاءَ
points: at the same time as an activity: أَثْنَاءَ الْأَكْلِ (while eating)

blocks.text: Dates: the day as an ordinal + مِنْ + the month: الْخَامِسُ مِنْ أَيَّارَ (the fifth of May), فِي الْأَوَّلِ مِنْ يَنَايِرَ (on the first of January). In speech the cardinal is common.

askYourself: Before or after? → قَبْلَ / بَعْدَ + genitive. In front of a place? → أَمَامَ instead.
Until? → حَتَّى + genitive; from … to … → مِنْ … إِلَى ….
Since / for, and still going on? → مُنْذُ + genitive, with the verb in the present.
During? The whole span → خِلَالَ; at the same time as an activity → أَثْنَاءَ.
At / on / in a time? → فِي (عِنْدَ for a moment), or the accusative alone: يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ, صَيْفًا.
Ago or in? → قَبْلَ + span / بَعْدَ + span.
Clock time? → السَّاعَةُ + a feminine ordinal; one o’clock السَّاعَةُ الْوَاحِدَةُ.
Which month names does my listener use? Levant and Iraq → the Syriac names; Egypt, Sudan, the Gulf → the Latin names.

traps: For “I have been living here for a year” use the present: أَعِيشُ هُنَا مُنْذُ سَنَةٍ.
*فِي يَنَايِرٍ → فِي يَنَايِرَ: a month name takes no tanwīn.
In standard Arabic the hour is an ordinal: السَّاعَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ, not *السَّاعَةُ خَمْسَةٌ.
حَتَّى and مُنْذُ take no pronoun endings in modern style; قَبْلَ, بَعْدَ, خِلَالَ, أَثْنَاءَ do (قَبْلِي, بَعْدَكَ).

quiz.why: Time: قَبْلَ + genitive (أَمَامَ is “in front of”).
Still going on: present + مُنْذُ + genitive.
The hour + a feminine ordinal, after فِي in the genitive.
قَبْلَ + span = ago; بَعْدَ + span = in; خِلَالَ = within.

quiz.q: Which is the Egyptian name of the month called آذَار in Damascus?

quiz.why: كَانُونُ الثَّانِي is January (a diptote: -a in the genitive); تِشْرِينُ الثَّانِي is November.
At the same time as an activity: أَثْنَاءَ + genitive.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew: לִפְנֵי (before), אַחֲרֵי (after), עַד (until — a cousin of حَتَّى), מֵאָז (since), בְּמֶשֶׁךְ (during); בְּ for at / on / in: בְּחָמֵשׁ, בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי. The month names שְׁבָט, אֲדָר, נִיסָן … are the twins of شُبَاط, آذَار, نَيْسَان.
German: vor, nach, bis, seit (+ present, like مُنْذُ), während (+ genitive, like Arabic); um / am / im where Arabic has one فِي.
Chinese puts 以前 / 以后 after the time (饭前, 饭后 = before / after the meal), uses 从 … 到 … for from … to, and says the hour with a cardinal: 五点 (five o’clock).
Lesson 14: the days, the parts of the day and the accusative of time (يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ, صَبَاحًا).
قَبْلَ, بَعْدَ, خِلَالَ, أَثْنَاءَ behave like أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ: an -a ending, the genitive, pronoun endings.

notes.text: Turkish saat (hour) and dakika (minute) are the Arabic سَاعَة and دَقِيقَة; but Turkish puts önce / sonra after the noun (kahvaltıdan önce), Arabic قَبْلَ / بَعْدَ before it (قَبْلَ الْفَطُورِ).
Swahili kabla ya (before) and baada ya (after) are Arabic قَبْلَ and بَعْدَ; saa (hour) is سَاعَة and dakika is دَقِيقَة.
Hindi puts time words after the noun — खाने से पहले (before eating), खाने के बाद (after eating), with बाद from Arabic بَعْدَ; Arabic puts قَبْلَ / بَعْدَ before the noun.
Persian قبل از / بعد از (before / after) are the Arabic words قَبْلَ / بَعْدَ; Arabic needs no از: قَبْلَ الْفَطُورِ.
Marathi puts पूर्वी / नंतर after the noun (जेवणानंतर, after the meal); Arabic puts قَبْلَ / بَعْدَ before it.
Japanese puts 前 / 後 after the noun (食事の前に, 食事の後で); Arabic puts قَبْلَ / بَعْدَ before it.
Finnish says ennen aamiaista (before breakfast, partitive) and aamiaisen jälkeen (after breakfast); Arabic: قَبْلَ / بَعْدَ + genitive, always before the noun.
Hungarian puts előtt / után after the noun (reggeli előtt); Arabic puts قَبْلَ / بَعْدَ first.
Vietnamese trước and sau come before the noun (trước bữa sáng), like قَبْلَ الْفَطُورِ; but the hour is a cardinal (năm giờ), where Arabic uses an ordinal (السَّاعَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ).
Inuktitut marks time with case endings on time words (the locative -mi); Arabic uses prepositions before the noun or the bare accusative.
